You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
The bug report indicates that StringUtils.containsAny methods do not handle Unicode 2.0+ supplementary characters correctly. The test that failed involves checking containsAny with supplementary characters (U+20000, U+20001). In Java, these supplementary characters are represented as surrogate pairs (two char values), e.g., "\uD840\uDC00" for U+20000.

Looking at the containsAny(CharSequence cs, char[] searchChars) method code snippet:

- It iterates over the CharSequence with cs.charAt(i), which gives a single char.
- It then compares each char with searchChars[j] (which are also char).
- If any char matches, it returns true.

This logic only works for characters in the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), which fit in one char. Supplementary characters are represented using two char (surrogate pairs). The method treats each char separately, thus cannot correctly match supplementary characters represented as surrogate pairs.

Hence, when checking containsAny with a supplementary character string and looking for a supplementary character in the array, the method will not find matches because it compares single surrogate halves separately rather than full codepoints.

The current test uses supplementary characters stored in Java as surrogate pairs. Because containsAny only compares char units, it cannot correctly handle supplementary characters and returns incorrect results.

Therefore, the root cause of the bug is that containsAny uses char-based comparison and iteration rather than codepoint-aware operations. It does not recognize that supplementary characters in Java Strings are represented as surrogate pairs and hence won't detect them correctly.

No relevant information from the recent bugs seems to relate to Unicode or StringUtils.containsAny, so they do not contribute additional insight here.

# Diagnosis

StringUtils.containsAny(CharSequence, char[]) fails to handle Unicode supplementary characters because it iterates over the CharSequence by char at a time and compares char values directly. Unicode supplementary characters in Java are represented as surrogate pairs (two char values), so treating each char separately misses these characters. This causes containsAny to incorrectly report no matches or false positives when supplementary characters are involved, as revealed by the failing test using supplementary characters U+20000 and U+20001. The method needs to be updated to handle supplementary characters by iterating over code points rather than individual chars.

Next step: Suggest locations for fixing this issue.
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.containsAny(java.lang.CharSequence, char[])

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
